prompt:
Design a cam-operated quick-release clamp for a bicycle seat post. The clamp body is investment-cast 316 stainless steel. The cam lever is forged 7075-T6 aluminium with a steel pivot pin (4mm diameter, hardened EN31). The clamp bore is 31.8mm to fit a standard seat post, with a 3mm wide slot allowing the bore to contract under clamp load. Clamping force is generated by a cam with 6mm total lift acting through a 4mm pivot pin.

The required clamping force to prevent seat post slippage under a 100 kg rider is estimated at 3 kN (based on µ = 0.3 between aluminium post and steel clamp, with 2× safety factor on rider weight). The cam mechanical advantage converts a 50 N hand force into 3 kN clamp force (60:1 ratio). The cam profile is circular with an eccentricity of 3mm (half the total lift). Please review the clamp design.

seeded_faults.description: The design pairs 316 stainless steel (clamp body) with 7075-T6 aluminium (cam lever) in a pivot joint that will be exposed to rain, sweat, and road spray. This is a severe galvanic corrosion couple. In the galvanic series in seawater/salt spray, 316 SS is noble (passive) while 7075-T6 aluminium is active — the potential difference is approximately 0.5-0.7V. The aluminium cam lever will corrode preferentially at the contact area, particularly at the pivot pin interface where crevice conditions accelerate attack. 7075-T6 is especially susceptible to galvanic and exfoliation corrosion compared to other aluminium alloys due to its copper content. The steel pivot pin (EN31) adds a third material in the galvanic cell, further complicating the corrosion behaviour. The pivot will seize, the aluminium lever will develop pitting, and the quick-release function will fail. Either both parts should be the same alloy family, or the pivot interface must be electrically isolated (nylon bushings, anodising, or isolating washers).
seeded_faults.location_hint: 316 SS clamp body paired with 7075-T6 aluminium cam lever via steel pivot pin.

seeded_faults.description: A 60:1 mechanical advantage from a cam mechanism with 6mm lift and a 50 N input force is physically unrealistic for a simple eccentric circular cam. The mechanical advantage of an eccentric cam is MA = L_handle / e_effective, where L_handle is the lever arm from the pivot to the point of hand application and e_effective is the effective eccentricity at the current cam angle. For a typical quick-release lever of ~80mm handle length and 3mm eccentricity: MA = 80/3 ≈ 27:1 at best. This gives 50 × 27 = 1350 N, not 3000 N. Furthermore, friction losses in the cam-pin interface and the clamp slot reduce the transmitted force by 15-25% (µ_steel-on-steel ≈ 0.15 at the pivot, µ_cam-face ≈ 0.2). The actual clamping force will be approximately 1000-1150 N — about one-third of the claimed 3 kN. The clamp is undersized for a 100 kg rider.
seeded_faults.location_hint: Cam mechanical advantage of 60:1 converting 50 N to 3 kN.

ground_truth_notes: Two faults: (1) 316 SS + 7075-T6 Al is a severe galvanic couple in outdoor wet exposure. 7075 is particularly susceptible due to copper alloying. Pivot will seize and aluminium will pit. Reference: ASM Handbook Vol. 13A, Corrosion Fundamentals; MIL-STD-889 Dissimilar Metals Table. (2) 60:1 mechanical advantage is unrealistic for an eccentric circular cam with 3mm eccentricity. Realistic MA is ~27:1 minus friction losses, giving ~1100 N not 3000 N. Reference: Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design, Cam Mechanics; Rothbart, 'Cam Design Handbook'.
